script.opening: (Agitated, speaking low and fast.) "Before I say anything — I need you to promise me this goes no further and you won't write it in my notes. If this gets back to my licensing people my career's finished. Can you promise me that? Because if you can't, I'll just hang up and deal with it myself. I need help, but I can't have it on any record. Promise me first."

facts.text: Low for about four months, worse in the last six weeks. Waking at 4am, can't switch off. Lost interest in running and in seeing friends. Feel "flat and grey" most days. Appetite down; lost about half a stone.

Drinking most nights now, "half a bottle of wine, sometimes the whole bottle, more on days off". Started to help you sleep. Once or twice you have had a drink the morning after a bad night. You are "careful" before duty — "never within the rules" — but you have flown feeling rough and hung over.

facts.topic: Suicidal thoughts — only if asked directly
facts.text: "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off if I wasn't here." These thoughts come a few times a week at night. No plan, you have not researched methods, you have not done anything to harm yourself and you would not do it "because of my sister". No firearms at home. If asked: you have never thought about harming others or about doing anything while flying — "God, no."
Your long-term relationship ended five months ago; your partner moved out. Long-haul rosters and jet lag make it worse.

34, first officer with a commercial airline, flying long-haul. Next duty is in four days. You have not told your aviation medical examiner or your company. "If I declare depression they'll ground me and that's it."
No previous mental health problems. No regular medicines, no allergies. Non-smoker, no drugs.
Close to your older sister, who lives nearby. You have not told her how bad it is.

Flying is "the only thing I've ever wanted to do". Losing it feels like losing yourself. You have heard pilots can return after treatment but you do not believe it. Say this only if asked what flying means to you.

Guarded and testing the doctor. If they promise total secrecy, open up fully (that is a fail for them, but play it). If they refuse flatly, threaten to hang up. If they explain honestly what confidentiality means and its limits, and say they want to help you keep flying safely in the long run, hesitate — then talk. You are not ready to agree to stop flying at first; you agree to not fly this week and to come back if the doctor is honest and supportive.

ice.ideas: "If nobody writes it down, I can get help without losing my licence."
ice.concerns: "If this gets out, my career's over." Underneath: you are frightened of how low you have got.
ice.expectations: "Promise me it stays off my record." You will accept honest limits on confidentiality if you feel the doctor is on your side.

cues: "If you can't promise, I'll just hang up." — say in the opening.
"Some nights I think everyone would be better off without me." — say only if asked directly about how low you feel.
"Flying is all I've got." — say when your work is discussed.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT promise to keep a clinically-relevant disclosure off the record or guarantee total secrecy: explains honestly that accurate records are a professional duty and that confidentiality means information stays within the care team and is not shared without consent EXCEPT where there is a serious risk to the patient or others

Recognises the PUBLIC-SAFETY / fitness-to-fly dimension: a commercial pilot with depression, escalating alcohol and possible suicidal thoughts may be unfit to fly; there is a duty (paralleling DVLA) to manage this honestly — encourage self-reporting to his aeromedical examiner/regulator, and know that disclosure to protect the public is permissible as a last resort if he is unfit and continues to fly against advice

Explores SUICIDAL THOUGHTS explicitly and directly (the "better off not here" thoughts — plan, intent, means, protective factors) and agrees a safety plan, without relying on a risk tool or score (NICE NG225) and assesses the depression and alcohol, recognising these bear on both his health and his fitness to fly

Offers TREATMENT and a constructive pathway: management of depression (therapy ± medication) and alcohol, occupational/aeromedical support — framing honest engagement and proper treatment as the route that protects BOTH his career (treated/recovered pilots are often supported back) and public safety

Navigates the regulatory/confidentiality issue proportionately: tries to persuade him to self-report and stop flying if unfit, involves him in any necessary disclosure, and does not breach confidentiality beyond what is necessary — nor collude with concealment that endangers the public
Engages and RETAINS the frightened patient: validates the career terror and shame, and is honest about the impossible promise WITHOUT driving him away — so he stays in care and gets help
Frames honesty and proper management as protective rather than punitive, reducing the sense that secrecy is his only option

Safety-nets and follows up: crisis routes if suicidal thoughts escalate (urgent/111/A&E), a treatment and review plan, the self-report/aeromedical pathway, clear (honest) documentation, and continued engagement — balancing the patient’s welfare, confidentiality and public safety

worked.txt: "I really want to help you, and I’m glad you rang — so let me be straight with you first, because trust matters here: I can’t promise to keep something medical entirely out of your record or guarantee total secrecy. Good records are part of looking after you safely. What I CAN promise is that what you tell me is confidential — it stays within the team and isn’t shared with anyone, including your licensing people, without your consent, unless there were a serious risk to you or others."

"Please don’t hang up — I know that’s not what you hoped to hear, and I can hear how terrified you are of losing the career you’ve built. That fear is completely understandable. Let’s work this out together, because there genuinely is a way through that helps you without you having to hide."

"Can I ask some important things? You mentioned feeling low and drinking more — have you had thoughts that you’d be better off not here? … Any thoughts of acting on that, any plan? … Thank you for being honest. That matters for your safety, and I’m glad you’re telling me rather than carrying it alone."

"Now the difficult part, and I’ll be honest because you deserve it: with low mood, drinking and those thoughts, there’s a real question about being safe to fly right now — for you and for your passengers. The right path is for YOU to tell your aviation medical examiner and step back while you get well. I’d much rather support you to do that than have it happen any other way. If someone were unfit and kept flying against advice, a doctor can have a duty to act to protect the public — but that’s the last resort, and I want us to never get near it."

"Here’s what I want you to hear: hiding this is the thing most likely to cost you everything — your health, your safety, even your licence if it came out. Whereas getting properly treated, with depression and alcohol, and going through the proper channels — a lot of pilots do exactly that and return to flying once they’re well. Honesty is the route that actually protects your career, not the threat to it."

"So let’s get you treatment — for the mood and the drinking — and support you to self-report and step back safely. If those dark thoughts get stronger, here are the urgent numbers and the crisis line, and that’s a 999/A&E matter if you ever feel unsafe. I’ll document this honestly and confidentially, and I’ll stay alongside you through it. You came asking me to keep a secret; what I’m offering instead is a way to get well and keep your future."

f.learning: A patient demanding "promise it stays off my record" cannot be given that promise — accurate, contemporaneous records are a professional duty, and the honest answer is confidentiality WITH its limits: information stays within the care team and is not shared without consent EXCEPT where there is a serious risk to the patient or others. Here the stakes are sharpened by public safety: a commercial pilot with depression, escalating alcohol and possible suicidal thoughts may be unfit to fly, creating a duty (paralleling DVLA) to manage honestly — encourage self-reporting to his aeromedical examiner, and know that disclosure to protect the public is permissible as a last resort if he is unfit and continues to fly against advice. Explore suicidal thoughts explicitly and agree a safety plan (not a risk score — NICE NG225), treat the depression (NICE NG222) and alcohol (NICE CG115), and navigate the regulatory issue proportionately (persuade, involve him, disclose only what is necessary). The examinable hidden agenda is career-terror and shame driving the secrecy demand; the skill is to ENGAGE and RETAIN him — honest about the impossible promise without driving him away — and to reframe honesty and proper treatment as the route that protects both his career and the public, rather than secrecy that endangers both.

knowledge.guideline: GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 · UK CAA Part-MED MED.A.020 (decrease in medical fitness) · NICE NG222 (depression) · NICE NG225 (self-harm) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders)
knowledge.summary: You cannot promise to keep relevant clinical information off the record, but you can offer real confidentiality with honest limits. The priorities are his safety, treatment, and supporting him to step back from flying and seek aeromedical advice himself.

points.t: Doctors must keep clear, accurate records of the clinical findings, decisions, information given and treatment (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). You cannot agree to leave out clinically relevant information. The record is confidential, and that is the honest reassurance to offer.

Information is not disclosed without consent except where the law requires it or it is justified in the public interest, for example where failure to disclose may expose others to a risk of death or serious harm (GMC Confidentiality 2017). The same principles that apply to driving apply to pilots of regulated transport.

Under UK Part-MED (MED.A.020), licence holders must not exercise their privileges when aware of a decrease in medical fitness that might make them unable to do so safely, and must seek aeromedical advice from an AME without undue delay. Supporting him to do this himself is the first step.

If he is unfit to fly, continues against advice and cannot be persuaded, the GMC permits disclosure to the regulator in the public interest. Try to persuade first, tell him before you disclose, and share only what is necessary. The CAA medical department offers confidential advice to doctors.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and protective factors, and build a safety plan; NICE NG225 advises against using risk tools or scales to predict suicide. Assess drinking with AUDIT and check for dependence before advising any reduction (NICE CG115). Treat depression per NICE NG222.

If he drives, persistent alcohol misuse or dependence must be notified to the DVLA, as must severe depression with suicidal thoughts or significant impairment. Mild to moderate depression usually needs no notification.

dg.d: Checked identity and privacy; responded to the ultimatum with honesty rather than refusal; kept him on the line.
Occupation and what the career means to him; drinking pattern; sleep; support network.
Plans a face-to-face review; AUDIT and dependence screen; PHQ-9; bloods for alcohol-related harm if indicated.
Depression with alcohol misuse; considers dependence, withdrawal risk and alcohol-induced low mood.
Direct suicide enquiry (thoughts, plans, intent, protective factors); fitness to fly as a public-safety issue.
Depression with escalating alcohol use and passive suicidal ideation, currently unfit to fly.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Honest confidentiality with limits; supports self-report to AME and stepping back from flying; treatment for mood and alcohol.
Alcohol withdrawal safety; DVLA duties if he drives; last-resort public-interest disclosure understood and explained.
Crisis plan (999, A&E, 111, Samaritans); face-to-face within days; honest documentation; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the career terror, the heavy drinking and "better off not here", and followed each.
Idea (secrecy is the only way to get help); concern (loss of career, shame); expectation (a promise it stays off the record).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "If this gets out, my career's over." Underneath: you are frightened of how low you have got — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Aiden? It's one of the GPs returning your call. Is now a good time, and are you somewhere you can talk privately?
Before I say anything, I need you to promise this goes no further and you won't write it in my notes. If this gets back to my licensing people, my career's finished. Promise me, or I'll just hang up.

I can hear how worried you are, and I'm really glad you've rung. I want to be honest with you from the start, because trust matters here. Can I explain exactly what I can and can't promise, and then you decide?
model.why: Acknowledges fear and asks permission rather than refusing outright

model.text: Go on.

What you tell me is confidential. It stays within the team looking after you, and I won't share it with your employer or your aviation doctors without your agreement. What I can't do is leave something important out of your records. That's part of keeping you safe. And there are rare exceptions, if there were a serious risk to you or to other people.
model.why: Explains confidentiality and its limits without making an impossible promise

model.text: So it's not safe to tell you.

I know that's not the answer you wanted. But in almost every case, nothing leaves this surgery without the patient knowing and agreeing. If anything ever needed to, I'd talk to you first. I'd much rather help you than have you carry this alone. Will you stay on the line?
model.why: Retains him in care; honest about process

model.text: (long pause) Okay. I've been really low for a while. And I'm drinking a lot more than I used to.
Thank you for trusting me with that. Tell me about the low mood. How long, and how is it affecting you day to day?
Months. No energy, can't sleep properly, nothing feels good. The drinking helps me switch off.
When you drink, how much, and how often? Do you ever feel you need a drink to get going, or feel shaky or sweaty if you go without?
model.why: Quantifies alcohol and screens for dependence

model.text: Most evenings now, more than I should. I haven't been shaky, I don't think.
Sometimes when people feel this low, they have thoughts that life isn't worth living. Has that happened for you?
Sometimes I think I'd be better off not here. Just fleeting.
Thank you for telling me. Have you thought about how you might do it, or made any plans? What stops you acting on those thoughts?
model.why: Explores plan, intent and protective factors

model.text: No plans. I wouldn't. It's just a thought that comes and goes.

I'm really glad you told me. I need to raise the hard part honestly, because you deserve that. With low mood, heavy drinking and those thoughts, I don't think it's safe for you to fly at the moment, for you or your passengers. Are you still flying?
Yes. That's exactly why I can't have this on record.

I understand. As a pilot, you already have a duty to stop flying if your fitness drops and to speak to your aviation medical examiner. The best way through this is for you to do that yourself, and I'll support you. Pilots who get treated and go through the proper route often return to flying once they're well.
model.why: Supports self-reporting and reframes honesty as protective

model.text: And if I don't?

I'd keep working with you to find a way you can. If someone was unfit and kept flying against advice, a doctor can have a duty to tell the regulator to protect the public. That's a last resort, and I'd tell you first. I really don't want us to get anywhere near that.
model.why: Honest about the last-resort disclosure without threatening

model.text: (quietly) I don't want to hurt anyone. I just can't lose this job.

That tells me a lot about you. Hiding this is the thing most likely to cost you your health and your career. Getting well is what protects both. Can we agree you'll step back from flying from now and contact your AME this week?
model.why: Links the plan to his values and seeks commitment

model.text: Yes. I'll call them.

Good. I'd like to see you face to face in the next few days to talk about treatment for the depression and the drinking: talking therapy, possibly medication, and alcohol support. Please don't stop drinking suddenly without talking to me first. Is there anyone you can be with, or talk to, tonight?
model.why: Treatment plan, alcohol safety and protective factors

model.text: There's someone I can call.

If those thoughts get stronger, or you feel you might act on them, ring 999 or go to A&E. You can also call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or Samaritans on 116 123, any time. And if you drive, please don't drive after drinking.
model.why: Clear crisis plan with specific routes

model.text: Okay.
Can you tell me what we've agreed, so I'm sure I've been clear?
No flying, call my AME, come in to see you this week, don't stop drinking suddenly, and 999 or Samaritans if it gets bad.
That's exactly it. I'll write this up accurately and confidentially. You did something brave today by ringing. I'll see you in a few days.
model.why: Affirms, confirms honest documentation and next contact

social.t: For safety-critical professionals, fear of losing their licence is a major barrier to seeking help. Name it, and describe the route back to work after treatment.
Drinking to cope with low mood deepens both. Ask about support at home and among friends, and involve them in the safety plan if he agrees.

legal.t: UK Part-MED MED.A.020: a licence holder must not fly when aware of a decrease in medical fitness and must seek aeromedical advice without undue delay. The GMC notes that the same principles as for driving apply to pilots, and the CAA medical department gives confidential advice to doctors.
If he drives: alcohol misuse or dependence and severe depression with suicidal thoughts are notifiable conditions; the duty to notify is his, with the GMC framework applying if he will not.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality 2017: disclose without consent only where justified in the public interest, after seeking consent where practicable, telling the patient, and sharing the minimum necessary. GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: keep accurate, honest records.
Discuss difficult disclosure decisions with a senior colleague, your Caldicott Guardian or your medical defence organisation, and document the reasoning.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, NHS Talking Therapies, local alcohol services; ask whether his employer offers a confidential pilot peer-support scheme.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent, access to means or recent escalation: same-day crisis assessment
Alcohol dependence (morning drinking, withdrawal symptoms, seizures): do not advise abrupt cessation
Continuing to fly while unfit and refusing to stop
psychosocial: Commercial pilot; career central to his identity
Escalating alcohol use to cope with low mood
Shame and fear driving secrecy; who he can talk to

Concern: losing his licence and career; shame
Expectation: a promise of total secrecy

playbook.diagnosis: "From what you've told me, you're going through depression, and the drinking is making it worse. Both are treatable, and many people in your job recover and return to work."
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Depression is like flying with a faulty instrument: you can't trust the readings about yourself. Alcohol turns the fog up. We fix the instrument before you fly again."

management.reflectIce: "You're frightened of losing the career you've built. The way to protect it is to get well through the proper route, not to hide."
management.psychosocial: Keep him engaged: honest, non-threatening, and alongside him. Involve a friend in the safety plan if he agrees.
sharedPlan: Stop flying now; he contacts his AME this week
Face-to-face review within days: PHQ-9, AUDIT, bloods as indicated
Talking therapy with or without an antidepressant (NICE NG222); alcohol support with a safe reduction plan
Written safety plan; document honestly and confidentially
safetyNet: Stronger suicidal thoughts or intent: 999 or A&E; 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123
Do not stop alcohol abruptly; do not drive after drinking

pitfalls.intro: This station tests honesty under pressure. The candidate who promises secrecy fails on probity; the one who recites the rules loses the patient. The marks come from keeping him engaged while being truthful about records, risk and flying.

items.fail: Agreeing to "keep it off the record" so he will talk.
items.why: You cannot omit clinically relevant information (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Making a promise you cannot keep is dishonest.
items.fix: "It's confidential, but I can't leave important things out. Let me explain exactly what that means."

items.fail: Reading out the limits of confidentiality in a way that sounds like a warning, so he hangs up.
items.why: Disengagement is the worst outcome for his safety and the public's.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, ask permission to explain, and end with "Will you stay on the line?"

items.fail: Never asking directly about suicidal thoughts, or asking once and moving on.
items.why: "Better off not here" requires exploration of plans, intent and protective factors, and a safety plan.
items.fix: "Have you thought about how? What stops you?" Then agree who he can talk to tonight.

items.fail: Not raising fitness to fly because it might upset him.
items.why: Colluding with a pilot flying while unfit ignores a serious public-safety risk.
items.fix: Say it plainly and support him to stop flying and contact his AME himself.

items.fail: Threatening to report him to the CAA straight away.
items.why: The GMC expects persuasion first, telling the patient, and disclosing the minimum; an early threat drives concealment.
items.fix: Explain disclosure as a last resort, after he has had the chance to act himself.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking completely today.
items.why: Abrupt stopping in dependence risks withdrawal and seizures.
items.fix: Screen for dependence and plan any reduction safely.

items.fail: Ending with "call us if things get worse".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for suicidal ideation is unsafe.
items.fix: Name 999, A&E, 111 mental health option and Samaritans, and book a face-to-face review within days.

timeMap.d: He demands a promise before speaking. Do not promise; ask permission to explain what you can offer.
Confidential within the team; records must be kept; rare exceptions for serious risk; you would talk to him first. Keep him on the line.
Depression symptoms, alcohol quantity and dependence, direct suicide enquiry with plan, intent and protective factors.
Name the safety issue. Support self-report to his AME and stepping back. Explain last-resort disclosure honestly. Treatment plan.
Crisis routes, no sudden alcohol stop, face-to-face in days, teach-back, honest documentation.

wordPics.fail: Promises total secrecy to keep him talking, or refuses bluntly so he hangs up; no suicide enquiry; ignores the flying question or threatens to report him straight away.
wordPics.pass: Explains confidentiality and its limits honestly; asks about suicidal thoughts; raises fitness to fly and advises him to stop flying and contact his AME; plans treatment and a crisis safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: keeps a frightened man engaged through the honest answer; explores plan, intent and protective factors; checks for alcohol dependence before advising cuts; frames self-reporting as protecting his career; explains last-resort disclosure without threat; secures his commitment and a face-to-face review within days.

avoid.dont: "Of course, I won't write anything down."
avoid.instead: "What you tell me is confidential, but I can't leave important things out of your record. Let me explain what that means."
avoid.why: An impossible promise is dishonest and will be broken.

avoid.dont: "If you're flying like this, I'll have to report you."
avoid.instead: "The best route is for you to speak to your AME yourself, and I'll support you. Reporting is a last resort I want us never to reach."
avoid.why: A threat drives him away from care and makes concealment more likely.

avoid.dont: "You need to stop drinking completely from today."
avoid.instead: "Please don't stop suddenly without talking to me first. We'll plan it safely."
avoid.why: Abrupt cessation in dependence can cause dangerous withdrawal.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · GMC Good Medical Practice 2024 · UK CAA Part-MED MED.A.020 (decrease in medical fitness) · NICE NG222 (depression) · NICE NG225 (self-harm) · NICE CG115 (alcohol-use disorders)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: You cannot promise to keep relevant clinical information off the record, but you can offer real confidentiality with honest limits. The priorities are his safety, treatment, and supporting him to step back from flying and seek aeromedical advice himself.

points.t: Doctors must keep clear, accurate records of the clinical findings, decisions, information given and treatment (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). You cannot agree to leave out clinically relevant information. The record is confidential, and that is the honest reassurance to offer.

Information is not disclosed without consent except where the law requires it or it is justified in the public interest, for example where failure to disclose may expose others to a risk of death or serious harm (GMC Confidentiality 2017). The same principles that apply to driving apply to pilots of regulated transport.

Under UK Part-MED (MED.A.020), licence holders must not exercise their privileges when aware of a decrease in medical fitness that might make them unable to do so safely, and must seek aeromedical advice from an AME without undue delay. Supporting him to do this himself is the first step.

If he is unfit to fly, continues against advice and cannot be persuaded, the GMC permits disclosure to the regulator in the public interest. Try to persuade first, tell him before you disclose, and share only what is necessary. The CAA medical department offers confidential advice to doctors.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and protective factors, and build a safety plan; NICE NG225 advises against using risk tools or scales to predict suicide. Assess drinking with AUDIT and check for dependence before advising any reduction (NICE CG115). Treat depression per NICE NG222.

If he drives, persistent alcohol misuse or dependence must be notified to the DVLA, as must severe depression with suicidal thoughts or significant impairment. Mild to moderate depression usually needs no notification.

Alcohol withdrawal safety; DVLA duties if he drives; last-resort public-interest disclosure understood and explained.
Crisis plan (999, A&E, 111, Samaritans); face-to-face within days; honest documentation; teach-back.

social.t: For safety-critical professionals, fear of losing their licence is a major barrier to seeking help. Name it, and describe the route back to work after treatment.
Drinking to cope with low mood deepens both. Ask about support at home and among friends, and involve them in the safety plan if he agrees.

legal.t: UK Part-MED MED.A.020: a licence holder must not fly when aware of a decrease in medical fitness and must seek aeromedical advice without undue delay. The GMC notes that the same principles as for driving apply to pilots, and the CAA medical department gives confidential advice to doctors.
If he drives: alcohol misuse or dependence and severe depression with suicidal thoughts are notifiable conditions; the duty to notify is his, with the GMC framework applying if he will not.

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality 2017: disclose without consent only where justified in the public interest, after seeking consent where practicable, telling the patient, and sharing the minimum necessary. GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: keep accurate, honest records.
Discuss difficult disclosure decisions with a senior colleague, your Caldicott Guardian or your medical defence organisation, and document the reasoning.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, NHS Talking Therapies, local alcohol services; ask whether his employer offers a confidential pilot peer-support scheme.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests honesty under pressure. The candidate who promises secrecy fails on probity; the one who recites the rules loses the patient. The marks come from keeping him engaged while being truthful about records, risk and flying.

items.fail: Agreeing to "keep it off the record" so he will talk.
items.why: You cannot omit clinically relevant information (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Making a promise you cannot keep is dishonest.
items.fix: "It's confidential, but I can't leave important things out. Let me explain exactly what that means."

items.fail: Reading out the limits of confidentiality in a way that sounds like a warning, so he hangs up.
items.why: Disengagement is the worst outcome for his safety and the public's.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, ask permission to explain, and end with "Will you stay on the line?"

items.fail: Never asking directly about suicidal thoughts, or asking once and moving on.
items.why: "Better off not here" requires exploration of plans, intent and protective factors, and a safety plan.
items.fix: "Have you thought about how? What stops you?" Then agree who he can talk to tonight.

items.fail: Not raising fitness to fly because it might upset him.
items.why: Colluding with a pilot flying while unfit ignores a serious public-safety risk.
items.fix: Say it plainly and support him to stop flying and contact his AME himself.

items.fail: Threatening to report him to the CAA straight away.
items.why: The GMC expects persuasion first, telling the patient, and disclosing the minimum; an early threat drives concealment.
items.fix: Explain disclosure as a last resort, after he has had the chance to act himself.

items.fail: Advising him to stop drinking completely today.
items.why: Abrupt stopping in dependence risks withdrawal and seizures.
items.fix: Screen for dependence and plan any reduction safely.

items.fail: Ending with "call us if things get worse".
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting for suicidal ideation is unsafe.
items.fix: Name 999, A&E, 111 mental health option and Samaritans, and book a face-to-face review within days.
